title: SHE WIPED HER MOUTH AND SAID, “I HAVE DONE NOTHING WRONG.” — THE TERRIFYING BIBLE VERSE ABOUT SIN THAT NO LONGER FEELS LIKE SIN
paragraphs: SHE WIPED HER MOUTH AND SAID, “I HAVE DONE NOTHING WRONG.” — THE TERRIFYING BIBLE VERSE ABOUT SIN THAT NO LONGER FEELS LIKE SIN

Proverbs 30:18–20 exposes something more frightening than adultery itself: a heart that has learned to sin without trembling, hide without shame, and convince itself that God sees nothing. But what happens when Jesus confronts the secrets we have become comfortable keeping?
There is a kind of sin that makes a person fall to their knees and cry.
And then there is a kind of sin that makes a person look in the mirror, straighten their clothes, smile at their family, open their Bible, and continue living as though absolutely nothing happened.
The second should frighten us.
Not because it is necessarily more visible.
But because it has become invisible to the person committing it.
Imagine this.
A woman returns home.
Her husband may be waiting. Her children may be sleeping. The house is quiet. Everything looks ordinary.
She washes her face. Checks her reflection. Perhaps answers a message. Perhaps prepares for tomorrow.
Nothing about her appearance suggests that something sacred has been betrayed.
And if someone asks whether anything is wrong, she has already rehearsed her answer.
“Nothing.”
Not a trembling confession.
Not a desperate plea for forgiveness.
Just one word.
Nothing.
The Bible describes a disturbing picture of this kind of moral indifference in Proverbs 30.
And the most frightening part of this passage is not merely what the woman did.
It is what she said afterward.
“I have done nothing wrong.”
Read that again.
Because somewhere between the sin and the denial, something terrible has happened inside the human heart.
And before you decide this article is about someone else's marriage, someone else's secret affair, or someone else's hypocrisy, understand something.
The Bible may be about to expose a place in your own heart that you have carefully avoided.
In Proverbs 30:18–20, Agur, the speaker in this section of Proverbs, says:
“There be three things which are too wonderful for me, yea, four which I know not:
The way of an eagle in the air; the way of a serpent upon a rock; the way of a ship in the midst of the sea; and the way of a man with a maid.
Such is the way of an adulterous woman; she eateth, and wipeth her mouth, and saith, I have done no wickedness.”
— Proverbs 30:18–20, King James Version
These are not random illustrations.
Agur begins with four mysterious ways: an eagle moving through the sky, a serpent crossing a rock, a ship navigating the sea, and a man with a young woman.
The Hebrew word translated “way” is דֶּרֶךְ (derekh).
It can mean a road, path, manner, or course of conduct.
In this passage, Agur is contemplating movements and relationships whose ways are difficult for him to comprehend or trace.
Then comes the unsettling comparison.
“Such is the way of an adulterous woman.”
The Hebrew reads:
כֵּן דֶּרֶךְ אִשָּׁה מְנָאָפֶת
Ken derekh ishah mena'afet.
Literally, “So is the way of an adulterous woman.”
The word מְנָאָפֶת (mena'afet) comes from the Hebrew root נאף (na'af), meaning to commit adultery.
Scripture is not describing an innocent misunderstanding or a harmless attraction.
It is describing a violation of marital faithfulness.
Then comes the devastating image:
אָכְלָה וּמָחֲתָה פִיהָ וְאָמְרָה לֹא־פָעַלְתִּי אָוֶן
Akhlah u-machatah fiha ve-amerah, lo fa'alti aven.
“She eats and wipes her mouth and says, ‘I have done no wickedness.’”
The word אָוֶן (aven) can refer to wickedness, wrongdoing, or moral evil.
Notice what the verse does not say.
It does not say that she confessed.
It does not say she was overwhelmed with remorse.
It does not say she recognized the devastation of betrayal.
It pictures someone behaving as though the wrongdoing were no more consequential than finishing a meal and wiping away the evidence.
That is the force of the imagery.
The text does not give us her name, her marriage history, her motives, or her eventual fate. Nor does it explicitly say that she had stopped feeling guilt altogether.
But it does show a chilling declaration of innocence where there has been wrongdoing.
And that is enough to confront us.
Because the greatest danger is not simply that people can commit sin.
It is that people can become skilled at explaining it away.
At first, there was hesitation.
At first, the conscience protested.
At first, the heart knew something was wrong.
Then came the explanations.
“I deserve to be happy.”
“My spouse doesn't understand me.”
“It's only a conversation.”
“Nothing physical happened.”
“God knows how lonely I am.”
“Everybody has secrets.”
“It's not hurting anyone.”
And eventually, what once required an excuse no longer seems to require an explanation.
But sin does not become righteous because we have become comfortable with it.
And silence is not the same as innocence.
A person can silence a conscience without obtaining forgiveness.
A person can erase messages without erasing accountability.
A person can convince friends that everything is fine while standing before a God who knows the truth.
And a person can become so practiced at pretending that even genuine repentance begins to feel unnecessary.
That is why Proverbs 30:20 deserves more than a quick reading.
It deserves an examination of the heart.
But we must be careful here.
This passage is not permission to condemn women while excusing men.
The seventh commandment says:
“Thou shalt not commit adultery.”
— Exodus 20:14, KJV
It does not say that adultery is wicked only when committed by a woman.
The same biblical standard applies to husbands and wives.
A man who betrays his wife and justifies himself is not morally superior to the woman in Proverbs.
A woman who betrays her husband and conceals it is not exempt from God's truth.
And a person who has never physically committed adultery should not assume that the subject has nothing to do with them.
Because Jesus took the conversation deeper.
In Matthew 5:27–28, He said:
“Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery:
But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.”
Jesus was not saying that lust and physical adultery produce identical earthly consequences.
He was exposing the fact that sin is not merely a matter of outward behavior.
The heart matters.
What we entertain matters.
What we deliberately cultivate matters.
What we do when nobody is watching matters.
And suddenly, the woman wiping her mouth is no longer a distant figure from an ancient proverb.
Her denial becomes a mirror for every person who has ever said:
“It wasn't really lying.”
“I only looked.”
“I was just venting.”
“I didn't mean anything by it.”
“I can stop whenever I want.”
“I'll repent later.”
Perhaps your secret is not adultery.
Perhaps it is bitterness you have been feeding for years.
Perhaps it is a private addiction that has slowly taken control of your thoughts.
Perhaps it is an emotional attachment you know is crossing boundaries.
Perhaps it is dishonesty hidden behind a respectable reputation.
Perhaps it is the resentment you nurture while publicly speaking about forgiveness.
Or perhaps you have become so accustomed to religious activity that you no longer notice how far your private life has drifted from the Jesus you publicly proclaim.
You know the worship songs.
You know when to say amen.
You know how to encourage someone else with Scripture.
You know how to post about God's goodness.
But there is a room inside your heart where you do not want the light turned on.
And you keep telling yourself:
“It's nothing.”
Yet the Holy Spirit may be confronting you with a question you cannot easily dismiss.
If it is nothing, why are you so determined to keep it hidden?
Not every private struggle is a secret sin. Privacy itself is not wrongdoing. And not every feeling of shame is evidence of guilt.
But when we knowingly protect what God has called us to forsake, we should not mistake concealment for peace.
Proverbs 28:13 says:
“He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.”
Notice both parts.
Confession.
And forsaking.
God does not invite us merely to become better at describing our failures.
He calls us to turn from them.
The biblical language of repentance helps us understand this.

The Greek noun μετάνοια (metanoia) means repentance, involving a change of mind and disposition. In the New Testament, genuine repentance is inseparable from turning toward God, as Acts 3:19 makes clear:
“Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out.”
Repentance is not simply feeling embarrassed because someone discovered the truth.
It is not crying because consequences arrived.
It is not apologizing while secretly planning to repeat the betrayal.
True repentance means acknowledging sin before God, turning away from it, and seeking to walk in obedience.
It does not mean a person instantly becomes perfect.
It means that instead of defending the darkness, the person begins walking toward the light.
And sometimes that is where the deepest struggle begins.
Because confession can be costly.
Truth may expose a carefully protected reputation.
A betrayed spouse may need time, boundaries, and honest answers.
Trust may not return quickly.
Consequences may remain even after forgiveness is sought.
And for some, telling the truth may mean finally admitting that the life everyone admires is not the life they have actually been living.
But hear this.
The grace of Jesus Christ is not permission to keep hiding. It is the invitation to stop hiding.
And there is another scene in Scripture that makes this truth almost unbearable in its beauty.
A woman is brought before Jesus.
She has been caught in adultery.
Her accusers stand around her.
Her sin is public.
Her humiliation is complete.
There is no carefully maintained image left to protect.
In John 8:3–11, a passage traditionally included in Christian Bibles, the scribes and Pharisees bring this woman to Jesus.
They want to trap Him.
They invoke the Law of Moses.
They ask what should happen to her.
And Jesus answers:
“He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her.”
— John 8:7, KJV
One by one, her accusers depart.
Then Jesus asks:
“Woman, where are those thine accusers? hath no man condemned thee?”
She answers:
“No man, Lord.”
And Jesus says:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
— John 8:10–11, KJV

There is an important textual detail worth knowing. John 7:53–8:11 is absent from several of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John's Gospel, and modern Bible editions often identify this textual question. Christians have long treasured the account, but we should be transparent about its manuscript history rather than pretending there is no discussion.
Its portrayal of mercy joined to a call away from sin is consistent with truths firmly taught elsewhere in Scripture.
And what a picture it gives us.
The woman in Proverbs says, “I have done no wickedness.”
The woman brought before Jesus has no such defense recorded.
One picture shows wrongdoing being denied.
The other shows a sinner standing before the One who speaks both mercy and truth.
We must not assume these are the same woman, or that Scripture is intentionally presenting them as paired historical figures.
They are not.
But read together, these passages confront us with two radically different responses to sin.
Denial says, “I have done nothing wrong.”
Repentance says, “Lord, I need Your mercy.”
And the Gospel announces that mercy is available because of Jesus Christ.
Not because adultery is harmless.
Not because betrayal is insignificant.
Not because God has lowered His standard.
But because Jesus came to save sinners.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we repaired our reputations.
Not after we became impressive Christians.
Not after we finally found a way to make our past look acceptable.
Christ died for sinners.
And that includes the adulterer who genuinely repents.
The liar who turns toward the truth.
The hypocrite who finally stops pretending.
The broken believer who has fallen and cries out for mercy.
The person who is terrified that God could never forgive what they have done.
The Cross does not declare that sin never mattered.
The Cross reveals just how seriously God takes sin—and how extraordinary His love is toward sinners.
Jesus did not suffer so that we could continue living comfortably in rebellion.
He died and rose again so that sinners could be reconciled to God and receive new life through Him.
That is why grace is so much more than a comforting religious word.
The Greek word χάρις (charis) is commonly translated “grace.”
In the context of salvation, it speaks of God's undeserved favor.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
You cannot purchase this grace.
You cannot earn it through public religious performance.
Salvation is God's gift through faith in Jesus Christ.
But the grace that saves us also begins transforming us.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace instructs us to reject ungodliness and worldly desires and to live godly lives.
Grace does not merely pardon.
Grace teaches.
Grace restores.
Grace changes the direction of a life.
And perhaps that is what you need to hear today.
Because there are two people reading this article.
One is hiding sin.
The other is still bleeding from someone else's sin.
To the one who is hiding:
You may have convinced everyone around you.
You may have learned how to delete the evidence, redirect the conversation, and silence uncomfortable questions.
You may even have convinced yourself that your choices are justified.
But God already knows.
Psalm 139:1 says:
“O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me.”
There is no secret He needs you to explain before He can see it.
And yet He calls you to repentance.
Not because He enjoys your humiliation.
But because sin destroys, and His mercy calls you away from destruction.
Stop calling darkness light.
Stop using pain as permission to wound someone else.
Stop confusing God's patience with His approval.
And stop assuming that because judgment has not arrived, accountability never will.
Today, you can begin telling the truth.
Today, you can confess your sin to God.
Today, you can seek wise pastoral counsel, end an adulterous relationship, establish necessary boundaries, and take responsible steps toward honesty and restoration.
If your situation involves abuse, coercion, or danger, seek qualified support and a safe plan rather than confronting someone in a way that puts you at risk.
Repentance requires truth.
But it does not require recklessness.
And to the person who has been betrayed:
Please hear this carefully.
Someone else's adultery is not proof that you were inadequate.
Their deception is not evidence that you were unworthy of faithfulness.
You may be questioning every memory.
Every affectionate word.
Every ordinary evening that now feels contaminated by what you did not know.
You may find yourself wondering whether you were foolish to trust.
You were not wrong to value faithfulness.
And you are not required to pretend the betrayal was small simply because you are a Christian.
Forgiveness does not mean calling evil good.
It does not automatically restore trust.
It does not eliminate the need for accountability.
And it does not require remaining in an unsafe situation.
Jesus cares about truth, justice, mercy, and the wounded.
You can seek healing without denying what happened.
You can pray for someone without immediately trusting them again.
You can place your broken heart before Christ even when you have no idea what restoration will look like.
And you can remember that the Savior who calls sinners to repentance is also near to those who are crushed.
Psalm 34:18 says:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.”
There is room at the feet of Jesus for the repentant sinner.
And there is room for the wounded person who can barely find words to pray.
That is the astonishing beauty of the Gospel.
It does not flatten every story into the same experience.
It does not erase the difference between wrongdoing and suffering.
But it offers hope in the presence of both.
Not about the woman in Proverbs.
Not about someone who betrayed you.
Not about the scandal everyone in your community still whispers about.
About you.
What have you been calling “nothing” that God has been asking you to surrender?
Perhaps you already know.
Perhaps the question brought a name to mind.
A habit.
A conversation.
A compromise.
A resentment.
A lie.
Perhaps your heart has been fighting conviction for months.
You still attend church.
You still believe in God.
You still love the idea of Jesus.
But you have been resisting His authority over one particular part of your life.
And you are exhausted.
Exhausted from maintaining appearances.
Exhausted from explaining things away.
Exhausted from being one person in public and another person in private.
What if today is the day you stop running?
What if the most important sentence you speak is not, “I have done nothing wrong,” but:
“Lord Jesus, I have sinned. Please forgive me. Change my heart.”
First John 1:9 gives this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not because confession makes sin insignificant.
But because the forgiveness of God rests on the saving work of Jesus Christ.
You do not have to defend what Jesus calls you to surrender.
You do not have to make your darkness look respectable.
You do not have to become worthy of grace before asking for it.
Come to Christ in repentance and faith.
Bring the truth.
Bring the shame.
Bring the broken promises.
Bring the parts of your story you wish you could erase.
And trust the Savior who died for sinners and rose victorious over death.
There is no biblical promise that every damaged marriage will be restored.
There is no guarantee that every relationship will return to what it was.
And genuine repentance does not erase every earthly consequence.
But there is a real promise of forgiveness and new life for those who turn to Jesus Christ in faith.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
That is not a promise that your past never happened.
It is the announcement that your past does not have to remain the master of your future.
Not because the scandal was imaginary.
Not because the wounds were shallow.
Not because the consequences disappeared.
But because Jesus rewrites everything.
He can take a life ruled by deception and teach it to walk in truth.
He can take a heart hardened by compromise and awaken it to repentance.
He can take someone who believed forgiveness was impossible and show them the immeasurable riches of His mercy.
And He can take a person who has spent years saying, “I have done nothing wrong,” and bring them to the liberating confession:
“Lord, I was wrong. And I need You.”
That is not the end of hope.
It may be the beginning of transformation.
We want these words to become invitations to prayer, encouragement, and honest Christian community—not public pressure to disclose what should remain private.
Someone reading the comments may discover that they are not the only person struggling to find their way back to God.
And perhaps your testimony, shared wisely and freely, will remind another person that repentance is possible and grace is real.
Not to embarrass anyone.
Not to expose someone's private failures.
But because somebody scrolling through Facebook tonight may be standing at the very edge of a decision that could change their life.
Someone may be about to destroy a marriage.
Someone may be trapped in a cycle of secret compromise.
Someone may believe they are beyond forgiveness.
And someone may desperately need to remember that Jesus Christ still calls sinners to repentance and offers them mercy.
Not because every sentence will be easy to read again.
But because there may come a day when you need to remember the difference between guilt that drives you into hiding and godly sorrow that leads you toward repentance.
We are here to proclaim Jesus Christ, encourage repentance, teach biblical truth, strengthen struggling believers, and point wounded hearts toward the grace of God.
Our mission is not to entertain people with religious controversy.
It is to help people encounter the truth of God's Word and grow as disciples of Jesus Christ.

You may choose to treat that support as part of your personal Christian giving, according to your convictions and commitments. It is a voluntary ministry contribution, not a biblical replacement for every believer's responsibility to prayerfully consider giving to their local church and other needs.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
We want it to come from a willing heart that values the proclamation of the Gospel.
These products can be reminders of biblical truth in everyday life, but they are not the heart of our ministry.
Jesus is.
We want the Word of God to reach people, regardless of their ability to give.
Pray for the people who will read it.
Speak about Jesus with someone who needs hope.
And live the truth you proclaim.
Because the greatest evidence of the Gospel's power is not how loudly we announce it.
It is how deeply Christ transforms our lives.
Before you leave, return with me to that unsettling picture in Proverbs.
A woman eats.
She wipes her mouth.
She says she has done no wickedness.
The verse ends there.
We are not told whether she ever repented.
We are not told whether she ever confessed.
We are not told whether she ever stopped pretending.
But your story is still being written.
You still have an opportunity to respond to God's truth.
You can continue defending the darkness.
Or you can come into the light.
You can keep saying, “I have done nothing wrong.”
Or you can bow before the Savior and say, “Lord Jesus, have mercy on me.”
And that difference matters more than your reputation, your public image, your religious accomplishments, or the applause of people who do not know your heart.
Because one day, the question will not be how successfully you concealed your sin from other people.
The question will be whether you have truly come to Jesus Christ in repentance and faith.
And for the person who does, there is mercy.
There is forgiveness.
There is new life.
There is grace.
The most tragic ending is not that your sin was discovered. It is that mercy was offered, and you chose to keep pretending you needed none.
